auth-oauth-passkeys.md:
## Why it exists
Two problems. First, apps want to act on your behalf at another service (read your calendar, post to your repo) without ever seeing your password: that is **OAuth 2.0**, delegated authorization. Second, apps want to know who you are without storing your password: that is **OpenID Connect (OIDC)**, an identity layer on top of OAuth that adds an ID token. A third, newer fix removes passwords altogether: **passkeys**.

Mental model: OAuth is a valet key (limited access, no identity). OIDC is the ID card the valet also hands you. A passkey is a lock that opens only for a key cut for exactly this building.

{{dg:0}}

## Roles and vocabulary
- **Resource owner:** the user. **Client:** your app. **Authorization server / IdP:** Google, Entra ID, GitHub, Auth0. **Resource server:** the API holding the data.
- **Scopes** are what the client asks to do (`calendar.read`). **Claims** are facts about the user in the ID token (`sub`, `email`).
- The **ID token** is for your app (proof of sign-in). The **access token** is for the API. Never use an ID token to call an API, and never treat an access token as proof of identity.

## Which grant to use
| Situation | Flow | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Web app with a server, SPA with a backend, mobile or desktop app | Authorization code + **PKCE** | The default for all user sign-in |
| Service to service, no user | Client credentials | Secret or signed assertion; scope tightly |
| TV, CLI, device without a browser | Device authorization | User approves on another device |
| Renewing access | Refresh token | Rotate, bind to the client |
| Implicit flow, password (ROPC) grant | Do not use | Removed or discouraged by current security guidance |

The IETF Security Best Current Practice (RFC 9700) requires the practical rules: PKCE for code flows, exact string matching of redirect URIs, no tokens in URLs. OAuth 2.1 is a draft that folds these into one spec.

## Worked example: authorization code + PKCE in Express
```ts
import { randomBytes, createHash } from 'node:crypto'
const b64u = (b: Buffer) => b.toString('base64url')

app.get('/login', (req, res) => {
  const verifier = b64u(randomBytes(32))                       // secret, stays on the server
  const challenge = b64u(createHash('sha256').update(verifier).digest())
  const state = b64u(randomBytes(16))                          // binds the response to this browser
  const nonce = b64u(randomBytes(16))                          // binds the ID token to this request
  req.session.oauth = { verifier, state, nonce }
  const url = new URL('https://idp.example.com/authorize')
  url.search = new URLSearchParams({
    response_type: 'code', client_id: CLIENT_ID, redirect_uri: REDIRECT_URI,
    scope: 'openid email profile', state, nonce,
    code_challenge: challenge, code_challenge_method: 'S256',
  }).toString()
  res.redirect(url.toString())
})

app.get('/callback', async (req, res) => {
  const saved = req.session.oauth
  if (!saved || req.query.state !== saved.state) return res.status(400).send('bad state')
  const tokenRes = await fetch('https://idp.example.com/token', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
    body: new URLSearchParams({
      grant_type: 'authorization_code', code: String(req.query.code),
      redirect_uri: REDIRECT_URI, client_id: CLIENT_ID,
      client_secret: CLIENT_SECRET, code_verifier: saved.verifier,
    }),
  })
  const tokens = await tokenRes.json()
  // verify tokens.id_token with the IdP's JWKS: signature, iss, aud === CLIENT_ID, exp, nonce === saved.nonce
  // then look up or create the local user by the stable `sub` claim, and start YOUR session
})
```
In practice use a maintained client (`openid-client`, Auth.js, Arctic) that does discovery, token validation and clock-skew handling for you; this code exists to show what those libraries protect.

## Passkeys and WebAuthn
A **passkey** is a **WebAuthn** (FIDO2) credential: the device generates a key pair per site, keeps the private key in secure hardware or a synced credential manager, and signs a server challenge after a local unlock (Face ID, fingerprint, PIN). The credential is scoped to your domain (the relying-party id), so a lookalike phishing site gets nothing to sign. That is why passkeys are phishing resistant while SMS codes and TOTP are not.
```ts
import { generateRegistrationOptions, verifyRegistrationResponse } from '@simplewebauthn/server'
const rpID = 'example.com'
const origin = 'https://example.com'

// 1) start: send options to the browser (navigator.credentials.create)
const options = await generateRegistrationOptions({
  rpName: 'Example', rpID,
  userName: user.email, userID: new TextEncoder().encode(user.id),
  attestationType: 'none',
  authenticatorSelection: { residentKey: 'required', userVerification: 'preferred' },
})
await saveChallenge(user.id, options.challenge)

// 2) finish: verify what the browser returns
const v = await verifyRegistrationResponse({
  response: body, expectedChallenge: await takeChallenge(user.id),
  expectedOrigin: origin, expectedRPID: rpID,
})
if (v.verified) {
  const c = v.registrationInfo.credential   // id, publicKey, counter: store all three per user
  await db.passkeys.insert({ userId: user.id, credentialId: c.id, publicKey: c.publicKey, counter: c.counter })
}
```
Sign-in mirrors it: the server issues a challenge, the device signs it, the server verifies with the stored public key. Use **conditional UI** (`autocomplete='username webauthn'`) so passkeys appear in the browser autofill.

## Strength of second factors
| Factor | Phishing resistant | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| SMS code | No | SIM swap, interception; last resort |
| Email magic link | No | Only as strong as the mailbox |
| TOTP app code | No | Good baseline; user can be tricked into typing it |
| Push approval | Partly | Prompt-bombing fatigue; use number matching |
| Passkey or security key | Yes | Best option; plan recovery |

## In real products
- 'Sign in with Google or GitHub' is OIDC. B2B products add enterprise SSO through SAML or OIDC federation per customer.
- GitHub, Google, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon all support passkeys; synced passkeys (iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password) recover when a phone is lost, device-bound keys give stronger guarantees for admins.
- Account recovery is the weakest link: a passkey is only as strong as the email or support flow that can bypass it.

> [!pitfall] Wildcard or prefix-matched redirect URIs let attackers steal codes through an open redirect. Register exact URIs.
> [!pitfall] Skipping `state` enables login CSRF: the attacker signs you into their account.
> [!security] Account linking by unverified email lets an attacker pre-register a victim's address, then take over when the victim later signs in with a provider. Link only on verified email, and key identities on `sub`, not email.
> [!tip] Put tokens on the server (backend-for-frontend) so a SPA never holds them. The browser only gets an HttpOnly session cookie.
> [!prod] The SimpleWebAuthn field names changed across major versions; pin the version and follow its README rather than copying older snippets.
q: An attacker who steals the authorization code cannot redeem it without the secret code_verifier that only the original client holds.
What is the difference between an ID token and an access token?
The ID token tells your app who signed in; the access token authorizes calls to an API. They have different audiences and must not be swapped.
The credential is bound to the real domain, so a fake site cannot request a valid signature for it, and there is no shared secret to type.
Why key a user's identity on the sub claim rather than the email?
Emails can change or be reused or unverified; sub is the stable identifier from that provider.

auth-passwords-sessions.md:
## Why it exists
**Authentication** answers 'who are you?'. **Authorization** answers 'what may you do?'. Confusing them is the root of many A01 bugs. This lesson covers the first: how to store passwords, how to keep a user signed in, and where **JWTs** fit.

{{dg:0}}

Mental model: a password proves identity once; a session is the wristband you get afterwards so you do not have to prove it on every request. Stealing the wristband is as good as stealing the password, so protect both.

## Storing passwords
Never store passwords, never encrypt them, and never use a fast hash (MD5, SHA-1, plain SHA-256). Use a deliberately slow, memory-hard **password hash** with a unique salt per user (the library handles the salt):
| Algorithm | Guidance | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Argon2id | First choice. OWASP minimum: 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, 1 lane | Memory-hard, resists GPU cracking |
| scrypt | Good. Work factor N of 2^17 or higher | Fine where Argon2 is unavailable |
| bcrypt | Acceptable legacy. Cost 10 or higher | Truncates input at 72 bytes |
| PBKDF2 | Only when FIPS compliance demands it, with a very high iteration count | Cheap for GPUs to attack |

```ts
import argon2 from 'argon2'
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto'

const OPTS = { type: argon2.argon2id, memoryCost: 19456, timeCost: 2, parallelism: 1 }

export const hashPassword = (pw: string) => argon2.hash(pw, OPTS)

export async function verifyPassword(hash: string, pw: string) {
  const ok = await argon2.verify(hash, pw)
  if (ok && argon2.needsRehash(hash, OPTS)) {
    // parameters were raised since this hash was made: store a fresh hash now
  }
  return ok
}

// breach check with k-anonymity: only 5 hex chars of the SHA-1 leave your server
export async function isBreached(pw: string) {
  const sha1 = createHash('sha1').update(pw).digest('hex').toUpperCase()
  const res = await fetch('https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/' + sha1.slice(0, 5))
  return (await res.text()).split('\n').some((l) => l.startsWith(sha1.slice(5)))
}
```
Current NIST guidance (SP 800-63B revision 4) favors length over composition rules: allow long passphrases and paste, screen against breached and common passwords, and do not force periodic rotation. A password used alone should be long (15 characters or more); shorter is tolerated only as part of multi-factor sign-in.

## Sessions with cookies
After login, generate a high-entropy random token, store only its hash in the database, and send the raw token in a cookie. A leaked database then does not hand out live sessions.
```ts
import { randomBytes, createHash } from 'node:crypto'
const sha256 = (s: string) => createHash('sha256').update(s).digest('hex')

export async function createSession(userId: string) {
  const token = randomBytes(32).toString('base64url')
  await pool.query(
    `INSERT INTO sessions (token_hash, user_id, expires_at)
     VALUES ($1, $2, now() + interval '7 days')`, [sha256(token), userId])
  return token
}

// login handler
const token = await createSession(user.id)   // always a NEW token at login: prevents session fixation
res.cookie('__Host-sid', token, {
  httpOnly: true,      // JavaScript cannot read it, so XSS cannot steal it directly
  secure: true,        // HTTPS only
  sameSite: 'lax',     // not sent on cross-site POSTs
  path: '/',           // required by the __Host- prefix, which also forbids a Domain attribute
  maxAge: 7 * 24 * 3600 * 1000,
})

// auth middleware
const { rows } = await pool.query(
  'SELECT user_id FROM sessions WHERE token_hash = $1 AND expires_at > now()', [sha256(token)])
```
Logout deletes the row, so it works instantly. Re-issue the session when privilege changes (login, password change, MFA step-up). **SameSite** blocks most **CSRF**, but for cookie-authenticated state-changing routes also check the `Origin` header or use a CSRF token.

## JWTs: what they are good for
A **JWT** carries claims (`sub`, `iss`, `aud`, `exp`) plus a signature. Servers can verify it without a database lookup, which suits service-to-service calls and tokens issued by an identity provider. Always verify against the provider's key set and check issuer, audience, expiry and the allowed algorithm:
```ts
import { createRemoteJWKSet, jwtVerify } from 'jose'
const JWKS = createRemoteJWKSet(new URL('https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json'))

export async function verifyAccessToken(token: string) {
  const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, JWKS, {
    issuer: 'https://auth.example.com/',
    audience: 'api://orders',
    algorithms: ['RS256'],   // pin the algorithm; never trust the token's own alg header
    clockTolerance: 5,
  })
  return payload
}
```

## Sessions or JWTs?
| Concern | Server-side session cookie | JWT access token |
|---|---|---|
| Revocation | Instant: delete the row | Hard: valid until it expires unless you keep a denylist |
| Scaling | Needs a shared store (Postgres, Redis) | Stateless verification |
| Size on the wire | Tiny id | Hundreds of bytes per request |
| XSS exposure | HttpOnly cookie cannot be read | Dangerous if kept in localStorage |
| Best for | Your own web app and API | Third-party APIs, microservices, IdP-issued tokens |

For a first-party web app, a cookie session is simpler and safer. If you need tokens, keep access tokens short (5 to 15 minutes) and use **refresh token** rotation: every refresh issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, and presenting an already-used token revokes the whole token family because it signals theft.

## Defending the login endpoint
```ts
import rateLimit from 'express-rate-limit'
app.post('/login', rateLimit({ windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000, limit: 10, standardHeaders: 'draft-7', legacyHeaders: false }), loginHandler)
```
**Credential stuffing** (replaying passwords leaked elsewhere) is the dominant attack. Layer the defenses: limits per IP and per account, breached-password screening, MFA, and the same generic error and similar timing for 'unknown user' and 'wrong password' so attackers cannot enumerate accounts. Password reset must use single-use, short-lived, hashed tokens, never security questions.

## In real products
- Most teams should not hand-roll this: Supabase Auth, Auth0, Clerk, Cognito and Entra ID run the flows above, and Auth.js or Lucia-style libraries cover self-hosting.
- Sessions usually live in Postgres or Redis with a sliding idle timeout and an absolute maximum lifetime.
- Apps show 'active sessions' with a revoke button; that feature is trivial with server-side sessions.

> [!pitfall] JWT algorithm confusion: accepting alg none, or verifying an RS256 token with HS256 using the public key as the secret. Pin the algorithm list in the verifier.
> [!pitfall] Storing JWTs in localStorage. Any XSS then exfiltrates them. Prefer HttpOnly cookies or a backend-for-frontend.
> [!security] bcrypt silently ignores bytes past 72. Pre-hash long inputs or choose Argon2id.
> [!tip] Hash upgrades are free: verify with the old algorithm, then rehash with the new one on successful login.
> [!prod] Treat the sessions table like credentials: hashed tokens, short expiry, index on token_hash, and a cleanup job for expired rows.
q: Why store the hash of the session token instead of the token?
If the database leaks, attackers still cannot use the stored values as live session cookies.
Why is a fast hash like SHA-256 wrong for passwords?
Attackers can test billions of guesses per second on GPUs; password hashes must be slow and memory-hard.
When is a JWT a better fit than a cookie session?
When many services or third parties must verify identity without sharing a session store, such as IdP-issued tokens for APIs.
What does reuse of an old refresh token indicate, and what should the server do?
Likely theft; revoke the whole token family and force re-authentication.
